# Coffee water stress


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

In the field, the triage comes from code in the domain project: feature
engineering and an ML model flag the nodes to watch or fix for one farm
and one day. The SLM turns that triage into a WhatsApp message for the
farmer, as the [scope](design/scope.ipynb) describes. This module
generates synthetic triage records, so that we can build and evaluate
the message side before the real triage exists. It generates them in
code, without a language model, so every record is valid and a seed
reproduces it.

## Dimensions

The task has three dimensions with three levels each. A tuple sets the
main item of a record: the kind of problem, its spatial pattern and its
severity. For `both`, the record holds at least one item of each kind.

<details open class="code-fold">
<summary>Exported source</summary>

``` python
DIMS = dict(problem=['water stress', 'equipment fault', 'both'],
            pattern=['one node', 'cluster', 'widespread'],
            severity=['early', 'moderate', 'severe'])
SEVERITIES = DIMS['severity']
```

</details>

``` python
test_eq(len(tuples(DIMS)), 27)
```

## Farm layout

A farm is a list of groups of nodes, each group sharing an irrigation
line. The names follow one of three schemes, drawn at random: greenhouse
benches (small farms, 4 to 16 nodes), blocks with drip lines, or
numbered plots (12 to 80 nodes). Location names are what the farmer
reads, so they never contain node IDs.

## Causes and onset

Each item reports what the data shows about its cause, never a part that
no sensor watches. For water stress, `soil_water` says whether water
still reaches the soil: `arriving`, or `none` with the time since the
soil last got water, which is never later than the start of the stress.
Water that stops arriving is the commoner case, about 70% of items. For
equipment faults, `fault` says what the data shows. Moderate and severe
faults are always missing data, by the scope’s definition of fault
severity. An early fault on a single node can also be implausible values
from one `sensor`, or a camera whose view has changed; on several nodes
at once, an early fault is missing data, since one shared cause is far
likelier than many sensors failing in the same way.

<details open class="code-fold">
<summary>Exported source</summary>

``` python
FAULTS = ['missing data', 'implausible values', 'camera view changed']
SENSORS = ['soil moisture', 'thermal camera', 'air temperature', 'humidity']
```

</details>

Severity also sets how long ago the problem started. `ONSET` gives the
range of days for each kind and severity. For faults it follows the
scope’s definition: no readings for 1 to 3 days is moderate, and more
than 3 days is severe.

The record gives the start as a phrase that the message can use as it
is, so that neither the teacher nor the SLM has to work out weekdays
from dates: since today, since yesterday, since a weekday within the
past week, or for a week or more.

<details open class="code-fold">
<summary>Exported source</summary>

``` python
ONSET = {('water stress', 'early'): (0, 1), ('water stress', 'moderate'): (2, 4), ('water stress', 'severe'): (4, 8),
         ('equipment fault', 'early'): (0, 1), ('equipment fault', 'moderate'): (1, 3), ('equipment fault', 'severe'): (4, 10)}
```

</details>

## Items

One item is one problem at one location. A `one node` item names a node,
a `cluster` item names a group, and a `widespread` item covers the whole
farm with more than 70% of its nodes flagged. `used` holds the locations
already taken in the record, so that two items never point at the same
group.

Messages give no counts, so a cluster or widespread item carries an
[`amount`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/coffee.html#amount)
word for the share of its group’s nodes that are flagged: all, almost
all (80% or more), most (more than half) or some (half or fewer). The
triage computes it, so that neither the teacher nor the SLM does
arithmetic:


## Triage records

[`triage`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/coffee.html#triage)
is the generator for
[`sample`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/synth.html#sample).
It builds the main item from the tuple, then adds random variation: the
farm and its layout, a day in the Brazilian dry season (May to
September), and up to two extra items. Extra items are never more severe
than the main one, and are single nodes or clusters. Together, the
single nodes and clusters of one kind stay below the widespread
threshold: on a small farm, two clusters that flag almost every node
would really be one widespread problem, such as a gateway fault. For
`both`, the first extra item is of the other kind. Items are sorted most
severe first, so that the message can keep their order. A node that
sends no readings cannot be flagged for water stress, so when a `both`
tuple is widespread and moderate or severe, its widespread item is the
water stress and the fault is the extra item. The record holds no
weather: in the field, weather is an input to the ML model, and its
effect shows in severity and in `soil_water`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/franckalbinet/edgeslm/blob/main/edgeslm/coffee.py#L101"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

## A test set

The test set has 10 records per tuple, 270 in total:

``` python
recs = sample(DIMS, triage, 270, seed=1)
test_eq(set(Counter(tuple(r['tuple'].values()) for r in recs).values()), {10})
```

Every record keeps the rules above. The main item matches its tuple, no
item is more severe than the tuple, items are sorted most severe first,
every location appears once, `both` records hold both kinds, no water
stress item sits beside a widespread fault that loses data, and the
single nodes and clusters of one kind never add up to a widespread item.
Each item carries the cause fields of its kind, and nothing else about
its cause:

``` python
items = lambda r: r['input']['items']
sev = SEVERITIES.index
for r in recs:
    t, main = r['tuple'], items(r)[0]
    test_eq((main['pattern'], main['severity']), (t['pattern'], t['severity']))
    assert all(sev(it['severity']) <= sev(t['severity']) for it in items(r))
    test_eq(len({it['location'] for it in items(r)}), len(items(r)))
    if t['problem'] == 'both': test_eq({it['problem'] for it in items(r)}, set(KINDS))
    ps = {(it['problem'], it['pattern'], it['severity'] != 'early') for it in items(r)}
    if ('equipment fault', 'widespread', True) in ps: assert all(p != 'water stress' for p, *_ in ps)
    assert all(_flagged(items(r), k) < _wide(r['input']['nodes']) for k in KINDS)
    test_eq([sev(it['severity']) for it in items(r)], sorted((sev(it['severity']) for it in items(r)), reverse=True))
    for it in items(r):
        want = {'soil_water'} if it['problem'] == 'water stress' else {'fault', 'sensor'} if it.get('fault') == 'implausible values' else {'fault'}
        test_eq(set(it) & {'soil_water', 'fault', 'sensor', 'likely_cause'}, want)
        if 'nodes_flagged' in it: test_eq(it.get('amount'), amount(it['nodes_flagged'], it['nodes_in_group']))
```

Records have one to three items, and farms range from a few nodes to
about 80:

``` python
Counter(len(items(r)) for r in recs), min(r['input']['nodes'] for r in recs), max(r['input']['nodes'] for r in recs)
```
